newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OLYMPICS-GREENS GIVE POOR MARKS TO SYDNEY.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-GREENS GIVE POOR MARKS TO SYDNEY.

text.p: Sydney Olympic organisers, who promised to host a genuine "green Olympics", received a lukewarm performance rating on Wednesday from an environmental watchdog.
A 41-page report by Green Games Watch 2000 gave Sydney a mark of five out of 10, or "barely a pass", for the city's progress in implementing its bid commitments.
The key concerns surrounded pollution, particularly air and water quality, and waste, the report found.
The Sydney Games watchdog used the plight of a threatened frog species to highlight its call for improvement.

Despite a commitment to protect them, rare green and golden bellfrogs were still under threat because of disruption to their habitat near the Olympic site at Homebush in Western Sydney, the report said.
Group spokeswoman Peggy James said Sydney's reputation as a competitive, world-class city would suffer serious damage if Games organisers shirked their environmental commitments.
"The key issue raised by the review is whether or not Sydney can deliver on its promises to the global community," she said.

As part of its successful bid, Sydney detailed its environmental targets, focusing on the design and building of the athletes' village, which will provide accommodation for 15,000 competitors and officials.
They included the use of solar energy, recycling of waste water and building materials, and maximising the use of public transport.
In the first in a series of annual reviews, the group gave a mixed rating for the construction authority responsible for building Olympic facilities.
In terms of energy conservation, the authority had performed well, but its record for water conservation, minimising waste, and air, water and soil quality was poor to very poor.
The performance in planning and construction and protecting significant environments was described as fair.
The report was commissioned and paid for by the New South Wales state government, which is underwriting the cost of staging the Games.
But New South Wales Olympics minister Michael Knight, who is also head of the Sydney Olympic organising committee, said the government disputed some of the review findings.
"We believe we are meeting all the guidelines...we are undoubtedly delivering the most environmentally friendly Games in the history of the Olympic movement, said Knight.
